demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson re-cuts the handbook in the kit's own rows; acme's managed stores cut the same text by rules of their own, so point acme at the kit's rows for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: Do it: edit both twins, then build and deploy a tagged worker
demos.purpose: The edit is one sed line per file. Make it in the worker alone first and run the test: this is the mistake the test exists for, and you should see what it says. Then make it in the twin and run the test again. The edit is one sed line per file. Make it in the worker alone first and run the test: this is the mistake the test exists for, and you should see what it says. Then make it in the twin and run the test again. Three tests fail, and the first message names both files and both pairs. The second says what the mistake would do to the lane: acme/cgst_act_2017.md, cut into 1,536 chunks by the worker and 390 by everything offline. The third is the pinned difference, now three windows against one. Now the twin: The worker on your lane runs the image a build pushed under a tag, and the tag is GIT_SHA: by default the checkout's commit, read with git rev-parse. Your edit did not make a commit, so a build with the default tag would push the edited worker under the commit's own tag, as if it were the kit at that commit. When that commit is the one the running worker was built from, the edit replaces the original image under its own name, and a later "redeploy the original tag" deploys the edit. The cell below therefore reads the tag the worker runs now, keeps it in ~/lesson82-orig-sha (written once, so running the cell again cannot overwrite it), and builds under that tag plus -c400. It names the service and the deploy script on purpose: without SERVICES=ingest the build is every one of the seven images, and without SCRIPTS=commands/lesson-12.5.sh the deploy is every service, all under a tag only the worker has. The build's own lines go to a log; the grep shows make's >> lines, the deploy's result and any error.

demos.heading: REST: which image serves, and how many tokens a new chunk is
demos.purpose: gcloud run services describe printed one line in step 5. Underneath it is the Cloud Run Admin API, and its service resource says more: the image in the service's template, the newest revision that is ready, where the traffic goes, and, one call further, every revision the service has kept with the image each one runs. Step 9's revert deploys one of those images again, so read them now, while the edited worker serves. The kit counts characters: the window is 400 characters, and the batcher estimates tokens as characters divided by 3. The embedding model counts tokens, and reads at most 2,048 of one text, cutting the rest unless told not to (lesson B.2 read that on Google's page on 7 October 2026). The largest chunk at 400/50 is GEN-003's first window, 368 characters. The cell cuts the handbook at 400/50 in memory, finds that window, and sends it to text-embedding-005's REST endpoint in us-central1, as the worker's client would, under the worker's task type. The response carries the model's own count beside the vector.

demos.heading: Reconcile: the ledger against the bucket, the index against the rows, the golden rows
demos.purpose: Lesson 1.8 ran the nightly walk: every object in the bucket against its ledger row in sources/. For each object, a generation the ledger already holds is ok; any other generation has its bytes hashed, and the hash decides. The bytes the ledger already names are a touch (record the generation, index nothing); bytes a claim indexed that the ledger never recorded are a backfill; bytes no claim holds are a reingest, which rewrites the object onto itself so the worker's own path runs again. Drift counts the sources the ledger had wrong. Nothing in either function reads the chunker. The walk compares names, generations and hashes of bytes, so it proves the ledger names what the bucket holds; it cannot prove which rule cut the rows. Run the kit's own planner over a stand-in lane, four nights in this lesson's life: Nothing in either function reads the chunker. The walk compares names, generations and hashes of bytes, so it proves the ledger names what the bucket holds; it cannot prove which rule cut the rows. Run the kit's own planner over a stand-in lane, four nights in this lesson's life: The second night is the case the walk exists for: had the re-issue's push been lost, the ledger would still name version 1 at generation 2, the walk would hash generation 3, find bytes no claim holds, and rewrite the object so the worker indexes it, cut by whatever pair the worker runs that night. The same bytes can be cut two ways depending on when they arrive. Now the real walk, the plan only, and the versions view after it: The ledger row is a summary. The rows are the evidence: the cell counts the handbook's rows by version and state, finds the longest current row, and checks whether two current rows hold version 1's vectors: NP-03, which the new rule left whole, and GEN-003, which it cut. Then it counts every tenant's current rows in Firestore and reads the Vector Search index's own count. The re-cut changed 544 vectors in the same index the questions search, so lesson 1.6's live gate, scoped to the handbook, is the check that matters. Every one of the ten rows asks about a real clause, and every real clause kept its text and its vector: what moved is the 544 windows of generated text beside them, now shorter and more numerous. The gate says whether the clauses still win.

demos.heading: Put it back: the original tag, version 1, the checkout
demos.purpose: The order matters. Deploy the original tag first: from that moment every document the worker ingests is cut at 2000/200 again, and nothing else can be cut at 400/50 while you work. Then upload version 1's bytes: the worker finds a version it retired 30 days or less ago and answers with the undo, flipping version 1's 283 rows back and retiring the new version's 555. The undo cuts nothing, so it would bring back version 1's chunks under either worker; the deploy is what decides how the next upload is cut. The tag comes from the file step 5 wrote, so a new shell is no obstacle. The order matters. The undo cuts nothing, so it would bring back version 1's chunks under either worker; the deploy is what decides how the next upload is cut. The tag comes from the file step 5 wrote, so a new shell is no obstacle. Expect back to ingest:COMMIT, the deploy's lines, the service's image back at ingest:COMMIT on a newer revision, and then make reindex's line: ingest_reactivated, version 1's key acme_497809ffbaa6..., 283 chunks, 283 reused, 0 embedded, 555 retired. Last, the checkout. The test runs once more so the kit you leave is the kit the course ships, and passes:
